newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: HAPPY BIRTHDAY MR BULLIMORE
In Perth, British sailor Tony Bullimore will celebrate his 58th birthday today, and says he plans to relax with his family and have a few beers.
Mr Bullimore is recovering from frostbite and a partially severed finger, following his dramatic rescue by the Australian Navy and Airforce in the Southern Ocean.
He was released from hospital yesterday after surgery on the finger, but is continuing outpatient treatment at Fremantle.
Meanwhile, one of the major tasks ahead for him is to sift through media and film offers from throughout the world, in an effort to recoup finances lost with his yacht.
His nephew Steven Mulvaney says Mr Bullimore worked hard for many years to be in a financial position to build the yacht.
DUBOIS THANKS RESCUERS
Rescued French round-the-world sailor, Thierry Dubois, has come face-to-face with the air crews who played a major role in his rescue from the Southern Ocean.
Mr Dubois was a guest at a special ceremony at Edinburgh RAAF base north of Adelaide, home of the Maritime Patrol Group.
Speaking at the ceremony, South Australian Premier John Olsen, said the air-crews had given the state and the nation a massive morale boost.
Federal Defence Minister, Ian McLachlan, said the crews would benefit from the rescue and the meeting with Mr Dubois.
ALICE SPRINGS CASINO SOLD
The sale of the Alice Springs Lasseter's Casino to a Malaysian Group is expected to be approved by half way through this year, pending probity checks.
Owners IOOF investments say the name of the group and the price is confidential.
The deal still has to be approved by the Foreign Investment Review Board, and an application for a Northern Territory gaming license also needs approval.
The casino, one of Australia's smallest with a turnover last year of 15-million dollars, went into receivership in 1993, and was put out to open tender in early 1996.
CASINO ON CHRISTMAS ISLAND IN TROUBLE
The multi-million dollar Christmas Island Casino Resort in the Indian Ocean is facing serious financial problems, with management admitting local gamblers are currently the only customers.
Union officials in the small Australian Territory are concerned the
Island's major employer will soon close down, forcing 350 people out of work.
The Christmas Island Workers Union will today apply to the Australian Industrial Relations Commission to secure wages and redundancy payments for the workforce.
Melbourne's Casino International Management may take over the resort from Casinos Austria, if Supreme Court action by the Casino's private owners is successful.
Casino manager, John Smith, admits the resort is losing money, with the lack of an advanced electronic banking system on the Island turning away high rollers who gamble large amounts.
He says the Casino has been operating with little income for two months, but maintains business will pick up and there's no danger of closure.
HIGHER EDUCATION REVIEW GETS POSITIVE RESPONSE
There's been a positive response to the Federal Government's higher education review.
Employment Minister Amanda Vanstone says the review will look into the effectiveness and development of Australia's high education sector.

The Australian Vice-Chancellor's Committee has welcomed the announcement, saying it's pleased with the diversity of backgrounds of committee panel members, and the breadth of the review's terms of reference.

AVCC Executive Director Stewart Hamilton says the review isn't just a narrow review of funding arrangements, but puts the issues within the broadest possible context, of higher education in the 21st century.
Former head of Sydney's Trinity Grammar School, Roderick West, will head the committee.
KOALA GROUPS AT ODDS OVER CULLING
The Australian Koala Foundation says it's opposed to plans by the Hunter Koala Preservation Society to cull 60 koalas in danger from a sandmining operation at Port Stephens.
The society says the koalas need to be destroyed because many have claumidia, and would infect clean koala colonies if moved away from the Tomago sandbeds.
It also says koalas are difficult to relocate because of their territorial nature.
But Executive Director of the Australian Koala Foundation, Deborah Tabart, says koalas are sucessfully relocated all the time.
IRC RECOMMENDS RETURN TO WORK
The Industrial Relations Commission has recommended a return to work to allow negotiations to resume in a dispute at one of Australia's biggest resource developments.
More than 600 contract workers walked off the job almost a fortnight ago at BHP's one-point-five billion dollar Hot Briquetted Iron Plant at Port Hedland in Western Australia.
The workers are seeking wage rises of up to 38 percent above award rates and a living away from home allowance of 500 dollars a week.
The Commission has recommended wages be increased by up to 19 percent above the award.
Union meetings will be held in Perth and Port Hedland at nine o'clock this morning to consider a return to work.
Contractors have offered an initial four percent payrise backdated to July as an incentive for the negotiations to continue.
HEAVY SCHOOL BAGS CAN CAUSE PROBLEMS
A leading physiotherapist says school children carrying large loads on a daily basis can result in permament damage.
It's claimed school children are being forced to carry bags up to 30 percent of their body weight.
Physiotherapy research by Western Australia's Curtin University shows many children carry heavy bags for more than 100-minutes a day.
Manipulative therapist at the University of South Australia, Mark Jones, says some school children are even carrying lap top computers in their bags, as well as their books.
He says the weight that children carry should be a weight that doesn't force them into an abnormal posture.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
